extracted.intended_audience: students, legislators, and readers of political philosophy/policy
extracted.subtask_description: Normative criteria and practical considerations for structuring households, distributing property, organising political offices, and educating citizens in a well-ordered city. Emphasises the proper allocation of roles, virtues, property, and institutions to preserve the city and promote happiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of acquiring wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: There are several principal methods of improving a fortune: (1) merchandise (sending commodities for sale by sea or land, or selling on the place where they grow), (2) usury, (3) receiving wages for work done (either in a mean art or mere bodily labour), and (4) producing things immediately from the earth or their produce (timber, metallurgy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some methods are more profitable, others safer. Practical contrivances (e.g., Thales' monopoly of oil-works; buying up all iron merchants' stock) can be gainful. Politicians should understand these methods because states, like private citizens, sometimes need to raise money and may use similar devices (monopolies, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ranking of arts by excellence
rubrics_metrics.description: Those works of art are most excellent in which chance has the least to do; the meanest are those which deprave the body; the most servile are those that chiefly require bodily strength; the most illiberal are those requiring the least skill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arts should be judged by degree of skill, independence from chance, and their moral/physical effects. This classification explains why some employments are considered more honourable than others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three parts of domestic government
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic government comprises three parts: the masters (household heads), the fathers, and the husbands; these have distinct functions in household governance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different relationships within the family (master/slave, father/child, husband/wife) require distinct modes of governance appropriate to their nature and roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of wives and children within a free household
rubrics_metrics.description: The wife should be treated as a citizen of a free state, while the children should be under kingly power; the government of wife and children should both be that of free persons but not the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This reflects the view that males are naturally superior to females except in unusual cases; fathers have kingly power over children founded in affection and seniority (comparable to Jupiter as 'father of gods and men').

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of the virtues of members over possessions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the due government of a family, more attention should be paid to the several members and their virtues than to the possessions or riches; greater attention to freemen than to slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The virtue and character of persons determine the well-being of the household/state more than material wealth; thus education and moral formation take precedence over mere property concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: All human moral virtues are present but differ by role
rubrics_metrics.description: All persons (slaves, women, children, freemen) possess virtues, but the virtues are not identical in species — they differ as suited to their respective stations; both governors and governed ought to be virtuous, but in different manners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance and being governed are different kinds; virtues must be appropriate to the nature and function (e.g., man's courage is commanding, woman's courage is in obeying). General definitions of virtue obscure these role-differentiated virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that governors be perfect in moral virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Those who are to govern ought to be perfect in moral virtue, since governing is the business of an architect and reason is the architect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because rulers' role is to shape and guide, they need a fuller measure of moral and rational virtue than those they govern; inadequate virtue in rulers prevents good governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training for slaves and artisans appropriate to station
rubrics_metrics.description: Slaves ought to be trained to the virtues proper for their situation by their master; slaves are not to be deprived of reason and in fact need instruction (often more than children). Artificers should have as much of slave-like virtues as their station approaches slavery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Education should be calibrated to function: slaves need restraint against idleness/fear so they perform their uses; masters are responsible for this training rather than abstract denial of slaves' rationality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits to making a city 'one' or wholly communal
rubrics_metrics.description: A city must be one in certain respects but not so contracted that it ceases to be a city (a city presupposes multitude and different sorts); making everything common (wives, children, property) risks reducing the city to a family or single person and destroying its nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is desirable only insofar as it preserves the city's existence and diversity. Excessive uniformity annihilates key features (occupational diversity, multiple persons). The good of a thing is what preserves it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rotation versus permanence in offices
rubrics_metrics.description: Among freemen and equals some form of alternation in governing and being governed is necessary (rotation in office), while continuity of government in the same hands may be better where possible for stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where equality is the norm, rotation prevents concentration of power; where continuity is feasible and preserves good administration, stability can be preferred. The legislator must balance equality and stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of collective ownership of family relations and property
rubrics_metrics.description: If wives, children, and goods are held in common, people will care for them less; family ties and personal care weaken, leading to neglect, confusion about kinship, and social disorder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collective property and communal family relations erode personal responsibility and affection; private ownership with common use (or limited communal practices) is preferable to total communism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of friendship and clear kinship for social stability
rubrics_metrics.description: Friendship is the greatest good for a city and best prevents seditions; ambiguous or communal family relations weaken friendship and amity and therefore harm the city's stability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws and institutions ought to foster clear personal ties and affections (recognised parenthood, private relations) because they underpin civic harmony more effectively than abstract communal schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific harms of communal wives/children schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: Communal wives and children would increase blows, murders, quarrels, reproaches, and incestuous relations; legal remedies and social norms rely on recognisable family relations which communal schemes undermine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These concrete social harms (e.g., inability to perform legal expiation for offences among kin, increased sexual impropriety) serve as strong practical objections to such communal proposals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best regime for property: private ownership with common use
rubrics_metrics.description: It is best to have property private, but to make the use of it common; private property encourages industry and gives scope for virtues such as modesty and liberality, while some shared uses foster mutual aid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Private ownership aligns labour with reward and promotes care; communal use of resources (as among friends or certain Spartan/Laconian practices) can be instituted by education and laws but full communism is impracticable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impracticability of total community of goods and need for empirical caution
rubrics_metrics.description: A community of goods so entire as to include everything is very difficult to establish; experience of colonies and communal experiments shows disputes and violence; legislators should consult long experience before adopting such schemes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legislator must examine historical practice and long experience; schemes that look specious in theory may fail badly in practice. Education, manners, philosophy, and laws together (not laws alone) make a city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazards of fixed magistracy and rigid class-office assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Settling the magistracy so that persons of the same rank are always in office is hazardous and a cause of sedition; distributing offices permanently to a class ignores the mobility of 'golden particles' of excellence and produces unhappiness among excluded groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection and tenure of office must account for human nature and avoid permanent exclusion of large parts of the population; inclusion and rotation are political safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislator's double consideration: country and people
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislator should have two things in view when framing laws: the country and the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws must be adapted to the particular resources and character of the land and populace; what is possible in one region (e.g., supporting large idle classes) may be impossible elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as an indivisible aim of political organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness cannot be added together numerically across classes; the legislator's aim should be the happiness of individual citizens — the whole city cannot be considered happy unless every individual or at least the greater part is happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies that make some classes (e.g., the military or artisans) unhappy while privileging others fail the legislator's purpose; distribution of goods and offices must promote individual flourishing.
